abstract: Present communication reports a simple method of preparation of ZnO–Cu nano composite, a reverse water gas shift (RWGS) type low-cost catalyst for electro-catalytic reduction of CO2. The composite catalyst has been characterized by EDX, SEM, EDX atom mapping and XRD. The observed distinct reduction peaks at − 0.7 V and − 1.1 V versus Ag/AgCl in cyclo voltammogram (CV) are explained by cathodic reduction of CO2 to CO preferably onto ZnO surface and electro-reduction of CO/CO2 onto Cu surface. This electro-reduction peak at low over-potential indicates formation of small molecular organic fuels like methane and methanol onto catalyst surface. A signature of methanol oxidation peak at 0.79 V versus Ag/AgCl is detected in the anodic scan of the CV at 5th cycle. The catalytic stability has been explained from chrono-amperometric study.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Large-scale reduction of CO2 to fuel is one of the promising routes of restoring CO2 balance and meeting energy need (Robert 2016). Reduction of CO2 to alcohol or gaseous hydrocarbon fuel is neither thermodynamically nor kinetically a favourable process. Thermodynamic barrier is overcome by use of solar energy (Photo-reduction) or by applying electrical energy (electro-reduction). But to overcome kinetic barrier, development of an efficient photo/electro-catalyst for CO2 reduction is required. This is a major challenge to arrive at the goal. It is known ZnO–Cu is a cost-effective industrial catalyst (Fujita et al. 1992) for chemical reduction of CO2 to methanol. But this requires a high temperature. Thus it is not recommended as an energy-efficient method.
Again, in spite of exhaustive studies on the mechanism of CO2 reduction by reverse water gas shift (RWGS) type catalyst, the role of ZnO in this catalyst is not well understood (Jianga et al. 2018; Christina 2014).
Among the most studied electro-catalysts/photo catalysts for reduction of CO2, the Cu-based materials (Hirunsit et al. 2015; Basumallick and Santra 2014), particularly Cu(I) oxide, has been studied exhaustively as a direct solar
energy-driven photo-catalyst. Photo catalytic reduction of CO2 to formaldehyde and methanol using Cu2O was first studied by Tennakone et al. (1989). Exhaustive experimental works on electro/photo-reduction of CO2 by Hori (2008), Andrews et al. (2013) and Yano et al. (2004) using Cu-based catalysts clearly established that such reduction, particularly reduction products, mainly depend on pH of the solution. This may be owing to the proton assisted (Bonin et al. 2014) electronation reaction.
We have studied (Basumallick and Santra 2014) electroreduction of CO2 using depolymerized chitosan-coated Cu2O nano catalyst and noted methanol formation. It has been also used as photo-reduction (An et al. 2014; Basumallick 2016; Richardson et al. 2011) of CO2 despite its instability and conversion to CuO.
ZnO is a low-cost material and chemically and photochemically stable. It is also used in combination with Cu as an industrial catalyst (Fujita et al. 1992; Le 2009) for reduction of CO2 to methanol (Le 2009; Hirunsit et al. 2015)
In this research, we report an easy method of preparation of ZnO–Cu nano composite catalyst, their characterization by EDS, SEM, EDX atom mapping and XRD. We have studied electro-reduction of CO2 by cyclo-voltammetric (CV) and chrono-amperometric methods with a view to understand the role of different components of the composite catalyst. * Srijita Basumallick

sections.heading: Materials and methods
sections.text: ZnO nano preparation: ZnO NMs of average size 50 nm have been prepared by simple literature protocol, mixing dilute (0.1 M) each of the solutions Zn(NO3)2 and KOH under vigorous stirring then washed precipitate and calcined at 50 °C.

sections.heading: ZnO–Cu composite nano preparation
sections.text:
The ZnO NMs so formed (10 mg) were dispersed in 30 ml of 0.01 M CuSO4 solution taken in a 100-ml container where precipitate of Cu(OH)2 is formed by adding dropwise dilute KOH solution. Then tartaric acid and NH2OH as reducing agent 50 mg each were added and stirred vigorously magnetically at room temperature (300.15 K) for I hour. The mixture was centrifuged and washed repeatedly with DI water and dried under vacuum. The particles were characterized by SEM, EDX and XRD analysis. Formation of uniform nano-composites may be explained by unique interactions (Leon and Shaw 2014) between ZnO domain and CuO domain of Cu(OH)2; this may be owing to almost same ion sizes of Zn++ and Cu++ ions.
Electro-reduction of CO2 has been studied using our earlier method (Basumallick and Santra 2014) by a Michrome mini Potentiostat–Galvanostat with glassy carbon as working electrode, Ag–AgCl as reference electrode and a Pt as counter electrode.
The dispersed mixed nano particle solution was deposited onto working electrodes by drop dry method. All experiments were carried out at room temperature (300 K) and the pH of the CO2-generated solutions was found to be5.5. All the potential values reported are with respect to Ag/AgCl reference electrode.

Figure 1 shows the Energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping of Cu (Red) and Zn (Green) of a ZnO–Cu crystal. The particles are seen as agglomerated particles with sizes ranging from 200 to 800 nm.
Figure 2 shows the EDX mapping of the sample placed on a glass slide with a carbon tape additive. The atom mapping for Zn and Cu is shown in the adjacent images. Atom percent ratio of Zn:Cu was found to be 37:3.8; the presence of Na, C, O, Si and Mg is coming from the support material.
Conventional SEM image of the composite is shown in Fig. 3. It is seen that both rod-shaped and spherical
particles of sizes 40–200 nm are almost uniformly distributed. The rod shaped particles are due ZnO. Agglomerated particles are also seen.
Analysis of XRD pattern (Fig. 4) of the mixed composite nano material shows the presence of distinct peaks at two-theta values 34.17, 46.36 and 77.16 which are close to poly-crystalline ZnO peaks, i.e. 34.40, 47.51 and 77.00 and are perfectly in agreement with those of literature data (Liao et al. 2011); this clearly indicates that during our preparation process impurities do not penetrate into the ZnO nano crystals. The observed broad peaks at 2θ = 41.04, 51.14 and 72.04 indicate presence of Cu nanoparticles (Liao et al. 2011) in the composites.

CO2 electro reduction onto Cu and Cu (I/II) oxide nano material has been studied by different workers (Basumallick and Santra 2014; Hori 2008; Le 2009; Wang et al. 2014) with analysis of reduction products which show methane and methanol are major reduction products. It is interesting to note that after 5th cycle, the CV diagram shows a small peak (becomes to some extent prominent upon enlargement) around 0.79 V versus Ag/AgCl which may be attributed to the signature of oxidation peak of methanol which is formed during CO2 reduction.
It should be mentioned that cathodic peak current density (ipc) for CO2 reduction is small of the order of micro ampere. It seems reduction kinetics is governed by the diffusion and adsorption of CO2 onto catalyst surface as indicated in chrono-amperometric study. Figure 7, represents current in ampere versus time curve of CO2 reduction in 1 M Na2 SO4 solution at an applied potential of 1.2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The observed initial fall of current with time may be due to adsorption of CO2 onto electrode surface and has been observed by other researchers too (Jiang et al. 2016). In the present analysis, it is also seen ZnO cites of this composites play a significant role in the reduction process of CO2. Based on these primary observations and literature information, we propose a model of CO2 reduction onto Cu–ZnO catalyst which is self explanatory and pictorially shown in Fig. 8.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
We have prepared relatively low-cost ZnO/Cu nano-composite electro-catalysts for electro-reduction of CO2 by room temperature chemical reduction of copper salt in aqueous dispersion of ZnO nano materials; the –OH functionalized ZnO nano materials act as capping agent of Cu nano particles and prevent its agglomeration. Based on CV peaks and available literature information on individual components of the composite, a two-step electro reduction process as a major path has been suggested: these are electro reduction of CO2 onto ZnO with formation of CO and reduction of the latter to small molecular organic fuels like methane, methanol onto Cu active centre.
